lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first letter already says he loves her books and her, setting the whole correspondence in motion.

lines.text: Sympathy is dear--very dear to me: but the sympathy of a poet, and of such a poet, is the quintessence of sympathy to me!
lines.note: Elizabeth's reply values a poet's sympathy as the quintessence of sympathy, showing the bond forming.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's spring promise to see her turns the letters toward a real meeting.

lines.text: I shall be ready on Tuesday I hope, but I hate and protest against your horrible 'entomology.'
lines.note: Elizabeth's protest against his 'horrible entomology' is a private joke about how he pins her words down.

lines.text: You tie me like a Shrove-Tuesday fowl to a stake and then pick the thickest cudgel out of your lot, and at my head it goes--I wonder whether you remembered having predicted exactly the same horror once before.
lines.note: Robert compares her criticism to tying him up like a Shrove-Tuesday fowl, a vivid private joke between them.

lines.text: It is very kind to send these flowers--too kind--why are they sent? and without one single word ... which is not too kind certainly.
lines.note: Elizabeth notices his flowers sent without a word, a concrete moment of his wordless care.

lines.text: I scarcely know how to write what is to be written nor indeed why it is to be written and to what end.
lines.note: Her overwhelmed letter before the Pisa journey shows the relationship becoming serious and painful.

lines.text: And since I wrote what is above, I have been reading among other poems that sonnet--'Past and Future'--which affects me more than any poem I ever read.
lines.note: Robert's reaction to her 'Past and Future' sonnet shows her work deeply affecting him.

lines.text: When I first saw you--I saw your eyes--since then, you, it should appear, see mine--but I only know yours are there, and have to use that memory as if one carried dried flowers about when fairly inside the garden-enclosure.
lines.note: Robert recalls first seeing her eyes, a private memory of their earliest meetings.

lines.text: Dearest, you know how to say what makes me happiest, you who never think, you say, of making me happy!
lines.note: Elizabeth says he knows how to say what makes her happiest, a clear statement of his effect on her.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth's memory of the chestnut tree and west wind recalls Robert's earlier letter.

lines.text: No, No! indeed I never did.
lines.note: Elizabeth says she never called anyone by such a name, making his name intimate and new.

lines.text: ‘Did I ever receive such a letter?’
lines.note: Elizabeth says she never received such a letter except from him, showing his unique place with her.

lines.text: At from half-past three to four, then—four will not, I suppose, be too late.
lines.note: Their final arrangements for leaving together end the long correspondence in action rather than words.
